overview.text: The Dutch Empire was a network of trading posts, colonies, and territories assembled by the Netherlands over several centuries. In the seventeenth century, Dutch commercial companies linked Asian, African, and American ports. The Dutch East India Company, or VOC, could make treaties and wage war, and it made Batavia on Java its Asian headquarters. The Dutch West India Company operated in the Atlantic. Profits from spices, sugar, and other goods were inseparable from conquest, coerced labor, and the trafficking and enslavement of people. The empire was therefore both a commercial system and a system of political control over communities far from Europe.

key_facts.text: The VOC was founded in 1602 and operated in Asian waters.
The VOC built Batavia on the site of Jakarta in 1619.
The VOC was authorized to wage war and administer territories.
The Dutch West India Company operated in the Atlantic trade.
Dutch colonial slavery extended across Atlantic and Indian Ocean regions.

overview.text: “Persian Empire” is a broad historical label, not the name of one unbroken state. It can refer to several empires ruled from Iranian lands at different times. The Achaemenid Empire arose under Cyrus the Great in the sixth century BCE and stretched across much of western Asia. More than two thousand years later, the Safavid dynasty united much of Iran and made Shiʿa Islam the state religion. In 1736, Nader Shah founded the Afsharid dynasty after ending Safavid rule; his conquests briefly reached into northern India. These states differed in their institutions, borders, and religious policies, so dates or rulers should be attached to the particular dynasty meant.

key_facts.text: Cyrus II helped found the Achaemenid Empire around 550 BCE.
The Achaemenid Empire lasted until the conquests of Alexander in the fourth century BCE.
The Safavid dynasty began ruling in 1501 and made Shiʿa Islam official.
Nader Shah founded the Afsharid dynasty in 1736.
The Afsharid state fragmented after Nader Shah’s death in 1747.

overview.text: Toyotomi Hideyoshi was a Japanese military leader who completed much of Japan’s late sixteenth-century reunification after decades of civil war. Following Oda Nobunaga, he extended his authority across the archipelago; by 1591, his campaigns had effectively unified Japan. He sought to stabilize his rule by separating warriors from farmers and restricting weapons among non-samurai. Hideyoshi also ordered invasions of Joseon Korea in 1592 and again in 1597 as part of ambitions reaching toward Ming China. Korean resistance and Ming intervention prevented conquest. The wars devastated Korea, and Japanese forces forcibly took Korean artisans, including potters, to Japan. Hideyoshi died in 1598.

By 1591, Hideyoshi had effectively unified Japan.
He ordered non-samurai people to surrender weapons.
He invaded Joseon Korea in 1592 and again in 1597.
Korean potters were forcibly taken to Japan during the invasions.

overview.text: Belgium is a sovereign state in western Europe that emerged from the southern provinces of the United Kingdom of the Netherlands. After an uprising in Brussels, a provisional government declared independence on October 4, 1830. An elected National Congress adopted a constitution in February 1831 and chose Leopold of Saxe-Coburg as the first King of the Belgians. The constitution established a parliamentary monarchy, though the early electorate was limited. Belgium later became an industrial power and eventually a federal state. Its history also includes colonial rule in Central Africa; the Congo became a Belgian colony in 1908 after a period under Leopold II’s personal control.

The National Congress adopted a constitution on February 7, 1831.
Leopold I became the first King of the Belgians in 1831.

overview.text: Theresa May was the United Kingdom’s Conservative prime minister from July 2016 to July 2019. She succeeded David Cameron after voters chose to leave the European Union in the 2016 referendum. Her government began the formal withdrawal process under Article 50 in March 2017 and negotiated a withdrawal agreement with the EU. Parliament rejected that agreement, making Brexit the central challenge of her premiership. May also led the Conservatives through the 2017 general election, after which they continued in government. She resigned as party leader in 2019, and Boris Johnson became prime minister. The United Kingdom actually left the EU after her premiership, in January 2020.

key_facts.text: May became prime minister on July 13, 2016.
She succeeded David Cameron as Conservative leader.
Her government triggered Article 50 in March 2017.
The House of Commons rejected her withdrawal agreement.
Boris Johnson succeeded her as prime minister in July 2019.

overview.text: Ancient Athens was a Greek city-state whose political experiments and cultural achievements shaped later debates about democracy, art, and empire. In the late sixth century BCE, reforms associated with Cleisthenes broadened citizen participation. By the fifth century, adult male citizens could speak and vote in assemblies, while women and enslaved people lacked those political rights. After the Persian Wars, Athens organized the Delian League but increasingly controlled its allies and their contributions. Under Pericles, the city built the Parthenon on the Acropolis as a temple to Athena. Athens also fought Sparta and its allies in the Peloponnesian War, which ended in 404 BCE.

overview.text: On December 7, 1941, Japanese forces attacked the U.S. naval base at Pearl Harbor on Oahu, Hawaiʻi, while the two governments were still engaged in diplomacy. Aircraft struck ships and airfields, sinking or damaging many vessels and killing service members and civilians. The battleship USS Arizona suffered especially heavy losses. President Franklin D. Roosevelt addressed Congress the next day, calling the date one that would live in infamy. Congress declared war on Japan on December 8, bringing the United States into World War II. The attack was aimed at disabling American naval power in the Pacific, but it instead prompted a major U.S. wartime mobilization.

overview.text: The Umbrella Movement was a series of large pro-democracy protests in Hong Kong in 2014. Protesters demanded a more open way to elect the city’s chief executive after Beijing proposed a process in which a nominating committee could screen candidates. Student-led demonstrations expanded into occupations of major roads and public spaces lasting about 79 days. Many participants used umbrellas against sun and rain and as shields from police pepper spray and tear gas; the umbrellas became the movement’s symbol. The demonstrations drew broad attention to Hong Kong’s promised goal of universal suffrage and to tensions over its political autonomy. The disputed nomination plan remained a focus of argument after the street occupations ended.

Protesters demanded genuine universal suffrage for the chief executive.
The occupations lasted 79 days.
Umbrellas were used as protection during police tear-gas and pepper-spray responses.

overview.text: The Great Famine, known in Irish as An Gorta Mór, struck Ireland from 1845 to 1852, when it was part of the United Kingdom. Potato blight destroyed the crop on which many poor rural households depended, while poverty and inadequate access to other food made the disaster worse. Starvation and disease killed large numbers of people, and mass emigration carried survivors especially toward Britain and North America. The crisis changed communities and Ireland’s population for generations. Government agencies gathered appeals for help and organized relief, but surviving “Distress Papers” document how widespread urgent need became. The famine remains central to Irish history and diaspora memory.

key_facts.text: The Great Famine is generally dated 1845–1852.
Potato blight ruined a crop on which many households depended.
Insufficient alternative food provision contributed to destitution and death.
Large-scale emigration followed, including journeys to the United States.

overview.text: The Reign of Terror was a period of emergency rule and political repression during the French Revolution, especially from 1793 to July 1794. France faced foreign war, internal rebellion, and severe political conflict. The National Convention created a Committee of Public Safety and a Revolutionary Tribunal, while the Law of Suspects widened arrests of people deemed enemies of the revolution. Executions and other killings spread well beyond Paris. Maximilien Robespierre became closely associated with the Terror, but power also rested in revolutionary institutions and other leaders. His arrest on July 27, 1794, and execution the next day marked the end of its most intense phase and the start of a political reaction.

key_facts.text: The Terror is usually dated to 1793–1794.
The Committee of Public Safety was established in April 1793.
The Law of Suspects was adopted on September 17, 1793.
The Revolutionary Tribunal tried accused counterrevolutionaries without appeal.
Robespierre was arrested July 27 and executed July 28, 1794.
